processing: Today the name covers tea from the Yixing hills, mainly green and also black. The green teas are fixed by heat, shaped and dried; the Tang tribute tea was a different product from anything made now.
harvest_season: Spring for the green teas, as with other Jiangsu greens, with the early pickings most prized.
appearance_dry: Varies with the producer; green lots are typically fine, dark-green strands.
appearance_liquor: Described as clear, with a pale yellow-green colour typical of Jiangsu greens.
appearance_wet: Typically tender green leaf, as with other spring greens of the region.
taste_profile: Known for a clear liquor, a distinct aroma and a mellow, full taste.

brewing.notes: These are usual settings for a Jiangsu spring green. Black tea from Yixing wants hotter water, close to the boil.

vintage_note: Green Yangxian tea is sold as the current spring harvest and is best within a year. Because the name is a broad regional one, check whether you are buying green tea or Yixing black, and which year; black tea keeps longer.
description:
Yangxian is the old name of Yixing, the town in southern Jiangsu better known abroad for its teapots. Yangxian tea is the tea of its southern hills near Lake Tai, and it matters mainly for its history as a Tang tribute tea.

The name works as a regional label today, not as one specific recipe. It is a registered certification mark, and local tea is mainly split between green and black. The tribute tea of the Tang would have been made and drunk very differently, so nothing on the shelf now can be called the same tea.

Expect a clear liquor, a distinct aroma and a mellow, full taste from the greens, and brew them gently with water around 80 °C.

Because the label is broad, look for the specific tea behind it: Yangxian Xueya is a modern green with its own geographical indication, and Shanjuan Chunyue is a newer local green that uses Yabukita crossed with local plants.
history:
Yixing tea is traced back to the Eastern Han, though the early record is thin. The firm history starts in the Tang: in 760, after Lu Yu praised the tea, the Changzhou prefect Li Qiyun petitioned the court and tribute began. In 772 a tribute tea office was set up at neighbouring Guzhu Mountain, and it later took on Yangxian tea as well. The poet Lu Tong wrote its best-known line of praise.

Under the Song, tribute production moved to Fujian and Yangxian became chiefly a commercial tea, though Su Shi still wrote of seeking its snow buds. Later dynasties taxed and licensed the trade, and Yixing held a tea licence inspection office in the Ming. In the late Qing, after the ports opened, Yixing black tea was sold overseas.
